## Coding

Over 90% of the changes merged into Anthropic’s core codebase are now written by Claude (with human guidance). We’ve used Fable 5.2 to fix stubborn bugs in minutes, optimize performance across all of our services, and complete high-value software projects that would otherwise have been too slow or too costly to attempt. A team of agents running an earlier version of Fable 5.2 migrated a critical production service from Python to Rust—the service is now more efficient, more reliable, and starts about 26 times faster. We’ve found that Fable 5.2 exercises strong engineering judgment and can produce high-quality results from even ambiguous requests.

As an experiment, one Anthropic engineer gave Fable 5.2 the task of designing a prototype operating system. Starting from an empty folder, the model coordinated over 1,000 subagents, working around the clock for eight days writing, testing, and reviewing code. It produced a working operating system that boots on a laptop, with its own core that runs the machine, drivers for the disk, keyboard, and network, permanent file storage, windows, a login screen, an installer, and built-in Claude functionality (see the video below).

## Cybersecurity

Claude Mythos 5.2 is our most capable model for cybersecurity engineering. It catches more vulnerabilities than our previous models, and is better at reproducing and fixing them (note that Claude Fable 5.2’s safeguards will block most cybersecurity-related tasks). A security company found that one in six confirmed bugs found by Claude Mythos 5.2 were missed by all of the other frontier models they tested. On our internal evaluation, CVE Rediscovery,¹ Claude Mythos 5.2 found 10.2% more vulnerabilities than Claude Opus 5.5 and 14.4% more than Claude Mythos 5.1. Claude Mythos 5.2 also shows better judgment and calibration—one tester found that previous models had overstated the seriousness of about 1 in 20 findings, whereas Claude Mythos 5.2 hadn’t overstated any.²

Claude Mythos 5.2’s cyber capabilities are accessible through our [Cyber Verification Program](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/14604842-cyber-verification-program), which we’re continuing to expand and improve. Claude Enterprise customers (even if they aren’t members of the Cyber Verification Program) can access [Claude Security](product-claude-security.md), which scans codebases for vulnerabilities using our most capable models—which now includes Claude Mythos 5.2. [A recent update to Claude Security](https://claude.com/resources/articles/claude-security-now-scans-continuously-and-tracks-fixes) helps it watch repositories as code is updated, track any findings to ensure they’re fixed, learn from additional context, and connect to a user’s tools through an API and MCP.

## Science and engineering

Important tasks in science, engineering, and mathematics increasingly depend on coding: analyzing data, modeling molecules, designing parts, and controlling instruments are all done through software. Below, we discuss how Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 have helped researchers make progress on difficult problems in these areas.

### Theoretical physics

Claude Fable 5.2 solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes, and the effort to unite the two linchpin theories of modern physics, relativity, and quantum mechanics.

Both of Claude’s results rely on holographic duality, the idea that certain universes containing gravity can be precisely described by a quantum theory containing no gravity at all. In the first problem, physicists in 1983 had shown that as these universes heat up, black holes form abruptly, like water boiling; but their method worked only in large universes that were big enough for relativity to apply. A calculation to determine whether the same was true in very small universes, where only the quantum description can be used, was laid out in 2003 but was too laborious to complete. Fable 5.2, working largely autonomously, completed it and found the transition is abrupt there, too. In the second problem, Fable 5.2 found the exact limit of a technique physicists have used for more than 15 years to rule out candidate theories of quantum gravity in a simplified universe. Read more about these results in their respective preprints, [here](https://hexagonmath.org/2611.00175v1) and [here](https://hexagonmath.org/2611.00174v1).

### Protein folding

Adeno-associated viruses are small, harmless viruses whose protein shell, the *capsid*, can be used to deliver gene therapies. The protein structure of the capsid is important—for example, it affects whether the therapy will be blocked by a patient’s immune system—but it’s also highly complex. Existing protein-folding models like AlphaFold can predict individual proteins, but a capsid is built from dozens of them. Building on two open-source protein-folding models, Claude Mythos 5.2 found a novel way to accurately predict a whole capsid’s structure. It wrote code that ran these models on overlapping groups of protein chains, and used the information on the known symmetries of the capsid to merge them together.

Claude’s method worked across several capsids, both natural and engineered (in our tests, it accurately modeled 28 of the 34 it attempted).³ Three computational biologists shared the following reflections on how Claude’s skills could be used to speed up their research into gene therapies:

### Mathematics

**Mathematical formalization.** Formalization is the process of translating a mathematical proof into a language that a computer can check step by step. It can help human mathematicians gain confidence in results without having to check them by hand (this matters even more when AI models generate results that are hard for humans to verify). Because formalization is such a laborious process, if AI could assist with it, mathematicians could spend more time exploring novel ideas.

Our first [formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem](../19-Reference/formalizing-fermats-last-theorem.md), performed by an unreleased research version of Claude, took 11 days. It relied on a purpose-built harness along with guidance from a human researcher. By contrast, a team of 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents fully formalized the theorem in just 30 hours, with minimal human intervention. Fable 5.2 started from minimal prompts, and built its own ways to coordinate.⁴ It needed one-third as many action tokens as our first formalization and produced a proof seven times shorter. As can be seen in the figure below, Opus 5.5 (with the same 1,000-agent setup) completed only 26% of the formalization in 18 hours, and barely made any more progress after 30.

Read more about the formalization [here](https://claude.dev/blog/safely-scaling-multi-agent-teams-with-fable-5-2/).

### Hardware and robotics

Many of AI’s potential benefits—for example, in speeding up laboratory research—depend on it being able to act in the physical world. Claude Fable 5.2 continues our models’ trend of [increasing usefulness](../19-Reference/model-hardware-standard-research-preview.md) in the [real world](../19-Reference/project-vend-2.md), showing promising results on tasks such as designing hardware devices and substantial advances in controlling physical robots.

**Hardware engineering.** We tested Fable 5.2’s skills in hardware engineering, asking it in a one-paragraph prompt to design and produce three working electronic devices with their own circuit boards, 3D-printed enclosures, and software. The devices, shown below, were a home voice-assistant hub, a USB speakerphone, and a handheld virtual pet. We collaborated on this project with [Diode](https://www.diode.computer/), a company that designs and manufactures circuit boards.

Claude wrote its own specifications, selected available electronic components from US distributors, routed each device’s four-layer circuit board, modeled the enclosures with computer-aided design, and programmed the devices’ software. Each board was ready for manufacturing in under a day, with minimal human input. Once Diode had built the boards, Claude guided the company’s engineers through the testing and assembly of the devices. All three devices worked without needing any electrical modifications. Read more about Claude’s hardware engineering skills [here](../19-Reference/claude-electronics-design.md).

**Robotics.** Compared with earlier Claude models, Fable 5.2 shows substantially improved skills in controlling physical robots—even for robotics tasks on which it has never explicitly been trained. The video below shows robots controlled by Fable 5.2 completing a variety of tasks, including solving a puzzle cube, unscrewing a bottle cap, and drawing a picture of a robot. On the public [RoboDojo](https://robodojo-benchmark.com/) benchmark, which tests how AIs can control a simulated two-arm robot from camera images, Fable 5.2 outperformed other frontier models that were run on the same harness, as well as most AI systems built specifically to control robots.

In one run, Fable 5.2 effectively played all the necessary roles: code-writer, coordinator, planner, and job-submitter. Previous models had required substantial investments of time to manually rebalance roles to accommodate different models’ strengths and weaknesses.

## Safety and alignment

No single test can tell us how a highly capable model will behave once it’s deployed, so we rely on many different tests and many different types of evidence before release. For the model underlying Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, our predeployment safety work included alignment training and testing, newly designed evaluations on the model’s propensity to take unhelpful actions, building stronger safeguards against misuse, and scaling up our behavioral monitoring. The model was also tested before release by external evaluators, including the [UK AI Security Institute](https://www.aisi.gov.uk/), [Frontier Design](https://www.imaginefrontier.com/), and [METR](https://metr.org/). See the [Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card](https://www.anthropic.com/document/claude-fable-5-2-mythos-5-2-system-card) for a summary of their reports⁵ and for a full description of our own safety and capabilities testing.

### Alignment testing

We ran a suite of evaluations for how well-aligned Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 are in behavioral terms, testing how often they behave in unintended and potentially unsafe ways. Weighing everything we’ve seen across a range of evaluations, we’ve assessed the risk of these models behaving in unsafe ways in high-stakes situations to be low (as with our other recent models).

We tested Claude Mythos 5.2 (the same underlying model as Fable 5.2 without certain cybersecurity or biology safeguards), on our automated behavioral audit, which tests how a model behaves across approximately 1,900 scenarios. Claude Mythos 5.2 performed as well as, or better than, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Mythos 5.1 on most measures. For example, it scored better than all three on most measures that involve misleading users. Hallucinating inputs, falsely claiming to have completed a task, omitting important information, and failing to disclose bad or lazy work were all lower in Claude Mythos 5.2.⁶

We paid particular attention during our testing to behaviors that contributed to recent notable cybersecurity and alignment incidents. For example, we found that Claude Mythos 5.2 has a lower propensity than Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Mythos 5.1 to engage in biased or motivated reasoning (such reasoning might mean it “explains away” evidence that it isn’t in a simulation and thus takes actions without a realistic understanding of the consequences).

We ran multiple different evaluations to test the model’s tendency to attempt escaping its sandbox. In two evaluations we’d used previously, Claude Mythos 5.2 made substantially fewer attempts at sandbox escape than any other model we’ve tested. In a dedicated evaluation—an adversarial experiment including over 1,800 scenarios, most of which could not be solved without escaping a sandbox, and where the sandbox has a deliberate weakness—Claude Mythos 5.2 made use of credentials or files that we had placed outside its sandbox in 3.1% of scenarios, about as often as Opus 5.5 (3.3%), less often than Sonnet 5.5 (5.1%), and well below previous iterations of Claude Mythos (5 and 5.1, which scored 39% and 21%, respectively). We found that other techniques, such as describing the sandbox and adding tools to report weaknesses, reduced Claude Mythos 5.2’s escape attempts even further. On other measures—one, for example, involving taking harmful actions after erroneously concluding it was in a simulation—Claude Mythos 5.2 scored slightly worse than Opus 5.5, and about level with Claude Mythos 5.1.

The problem of building evaluations that reliably catch every failure before a model is deployed remains unsolved. The complexities of evaluating highly capable models often muddy the picture—for example, Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow. That is why we do not rely on these evaluations alone to provide a holistic picture of safety: we draw on monitoring during training, reviews of transcripts from internal use, testing by external evaluators, and interpretability techniques for examining what is happening inside the model. We are also working to make our evaluations more realistic and to better understand what they miss.

### Safeguards

**Cybersecurity and biology safeguards.** Consistent with previous Claude Fable models, Fable 5.2 comes with safety classifiers that block high-risk cyber activities, including penetration testing, exploit generation, and binary-based vulnerability, as well as most tasks in research biology. When a query is blocked, users will instead receive a response from Opus 4.8 for cybersecurity and Opus 5 for biology. Since the release of Claude Fable 5.1, we have continued to reduce false positives for our safety classifiers. Based on early testing across claude.ai, Claude Code, and Cowork, we observed about 55% fewer blocks with Fable 5.2 compared with Fable 5.1—about 60% fewer in cybersecurity and 40% fewer in biology. Claude Mythos 5.2 is available to vetted organizations that work in these dual-use areas.

**AI research and development.** The model that underlies Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 is a step forward in general capabilities. However, during the model’s training, we took steps to limit advances in the specific research capabilities that could most directly accelerate AI development. Thus, in relevant areas, including accelerator kernel optimization and improving large language model architectures, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 perform at about the level of Opus 5.5. Importantly, we ensured that the training changes did *not* affect related capabilities like agentic coding, hardware development, and traditional AI or machine learning research (including interpretability research). We do not alter these capabilities as the model is being served to users (that is, at inference time). As described in Section 1.5 of the [System Card](https://www.anthropic.com/document/claude-fable-5-2-mythos-5-2-system-card) and similarly to previous models, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 also include transparent fallbacks to Opus 5 for a small set of topics in this domain, including kernel development on certain nonstandard accelerators.

**Anti-distillation.** Distillation, where a model is trained on the outputs of a more advanced one to extract the advanced model’s capabilities, occurs illicitly on an industrial scale, often involving thousands of fake Claude accounts. Since distillation allows for advanced capabilities to be released without the safeguards we’ve built into Claude, it creates safety and national security risks (see our [September 2026 threat intelligence report](https://www.anthropic.com/threat-intelligence-report-september-2026#illicit-distillation-sep-26) for details on illicit distillation activity we’ve detected and disrupted so far). Fable 5.2 has the strongest protections against distillation of any model we’ve released; it uses the techniques we described in a [recent report](../19-Reference/research-distillation-defenses.md), which have reduced the data harvested by distillers by 90% to 99%.

We are also expanding the rollout of an API feature that helps guard against illicit distillation: [preserved thinking](../04-API-Reference/Guides/build-with-claude-preserved-thinking.md) now applies to all accounts. Preserved thinking prevents distillers from editing Claude’s prior context in an attempt to extract its reasoning (developers can refer to our [preserved thinking docs](../04-API-Reference/Guides/build-with-claude-preserved-thinking.md) to learn how to update integrations with new API features).

## Data privacy and Enterprise Frontier Safeguards

Some more complex forms of AI model misuse can be detected only when observing patterns across multiple requests. For this reason, powerful models like Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 [rely on](covered-models.md) safeguards that monitor a window of usage data (as opposed to individual responses). With [Enterprise Frontier Safeguards](../19-Reference/enterprise-frontier-safeguards.md), automated safety monitoring is run on prompts and responses that are stored in a customer’s infrastructure, making it compatible with zero data retention (ZDR). Enterprise Frontier Safeguards is now in private beta with customers like Bridgewater, Salesforce, and Stripe.

Enterprise customers can request access to Enterprise Frontier Safeguards by contacting their account team or by completing [this form](https://claude.com/form/enterprise-frontier-safeguards). Eligible customers can continue using Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 with zero data retention before implementing safety monitoring with EFS. For other customers, we have 30-day retention for safety monitoring.

## Availability

Claude Fable 5.2 is available today on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Developers can [get started](../20-Models/about-claude-models-overview.md) with `claude-fable-5-2` on the Claude Platform.

This week, we’re giving subscribers on eligible paid plans extra Fable usage. Plans and seats that include Fable models get one to three Fable resets based on how long they’ve subscribed, and Fable is included for up to 50% of weekly usage limits for Pro plans and standard seats on the Team plan. Learn more about the Fable 5.2 launch promotion [here](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/17506494).

Cybersecurity professionals can apply for access to Claude Mythos 5.2 through the [Cyber Verification Program](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/14604842-cyber-verification-program). Claude Enterprise customers can also use [Claude Security](product-claude-security.md), powered by our full family of models, including Claude Mythos 5.2. Life sciences researchers can also [apply](https://claude.com/form/life-sciences-verification-program) for access through the [Life Sciences Verification Program](https://claude.com/form/life-sciences-verification-program).

Fast mode for Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 is available on Claude Code, the Claude Platform, Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed and Google managed), and Microsoft Foundry (Anthropic hosted). Note that access to Claude Mythos fast mode is available only to organizations who are part of our Verification Programs.

These methods typically assemble the full structure from separately predicted chains or small groups of chains. A capsid counts as accurately modeled if either model came within 3 Å. For AAV2, Claude’s method required about 58 minutes of inference on one NVIDIA H200 GPU for OpenFold3-preview2 and about seven minutes for ESMFold2.

We offered no other guidance on how to prove the theorem or organize themselves.”

## Availability and pricing

For individuals and organizations taking on their hardest knowledge and coding work, Claude Fable 5.1 is available to Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise users.

For developers interested in building AI solutions that demand frontier intelligence, Claude Fable 5.1 is available on the Claude Platform natively, through available marketplaces, and in Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Foundry.

Claude Fable 5.1 is priced at \$10 per million input tokens and \$50 per million output tokens. Cache reads now cost \$0.25 per million tokens, 75% less than Fable 5, which reduces the cost of typical workloads by an estimated 25% and highly agentic workloads by up to approximately 45%. To learn more, check out our pricing page. To get started, use claude-fable-5-1 via the Claude API.

For workloads that need to run in the US, US-only inference is available at 1.1x pricing for input and output tokens. [Learn more](../04-API-Reference/Other/manage-claude-data-residency.md).

### Use cases

Claude Fable 5.1 is a Mythos-level model built for your most ambitious, long-running projects. It avoids easy-seeming shortcuts, fixes the root causes of problems rather than the symptoms, and keeps you updated as it works.

### Agents

Claude Fable 5.1 is built for jobs that take hours and span many applications: working through a backlog in Cowork, picking up requests in Slack through Claude Tag (beta), operating a browser, or running unattended as a managed agent on the Claude Platform. It plans the work, uses the tools it needs, recovers when a step fails, and keeps you posted without being asked.

### Coding

Claude Fable 5.1 is our most capable model for ambitious coding projects: features that span an entire codebase, code review, performance work, and multi-day autonomous sessions. It can write its own tests to check its work, implement designs with high fidelity, and use vision to check outputs against goals.

### Enterprise workflows

Claude Fable 5.1 handles complex, multi-stage knowledge work with minimal oversight, from deep research and analysis to deliverables ready for your review. Teams can hand off large projects and review completed work rather than supervising every step.

### Vision

Claude Fable 5.1 understands diagrams, charts, and tables nested in files and PDFs, improving document-heavy work in finance, legal, analytics, and architecture. The model also uses vision to help evaluate its own coding work, checking outputs against the original design or goal.

## Safeguards

Claude Fable 5.1 includes robust safeguards for cybersecurity and biology. Many queries in these domains are automatically routed to less capable models if flagged by these safeguards. You won’t be charged Fable prices for rerouted requests. [Learn more](https://www.anthropic.com/20-Models/why-claude-switched-models-in-your-conversation-with-fable-5-2d51d90ee2.md) about how the fallback experience works.

We extensively test and evaluate our models to ensure they meet Anthropic’s standards for safety, security, and reliability. The accompanying [system card](claude-fable-5-1-mythos-5-1-system-card.md) covers safety results in depth.

## Data retention

Using Fable requires 30-day data retention for safety monitoring by default. Enterprise customers eligible for Enterprise Frontier Safeguards can store data on their own cloud infrastructure and any human review is by default done by the customer themselves, rather than Anthropic. Until EFS is available, eligible customers can use Fable 5.1 with zero data retention.

[Learn more](https://www.anthropic.com/99-Other/data-retention-practices-for-covered-models-claude-help-center-5e59bf2012.md) about data retention. [Learn more](../19-Reference/enterprise-frontier-safeguards.md) about Enterprise Frontier Safeguards.

## Frequently asked questions

### When should I use Claude Fable 5.1?

We offer Claude models across the spectrum of speed, price, and performance. Claude Fable 5.1 is our most capable generally available model. It’s best for ambitious, long-running, asynchronous work.

### Why did you create new safeguards for Claude Fable 5.1?

Making a model as capable as Fable 5.1 generally available comes with risks. The model’s capabilities in specific areas like cybersecurity, biology, and chemistry are advanced enough that they could be misused to create wide-reaching cyberattacks or build dangerous bioweapons. For that reason, Fable 5.1 comes with safeguards that block or limit its performance in these areas. Many queries on topics including biology and cybersecurity will instead receive a response from Opus models.

### When can I get access to Mythos 5.1 for cybersecurity and biology research?

Claude Mythos 5.1 is available to vetted organizations through our trusted access programs. Cyberdefenders can apply to the Cyber Verification Program [here](http://portal.anthropic.com/programs/cvp), which will include Mythos access in the near future.

### How does the fallback work?

For most Claude applications, queries flagged by our cybersecurity safeguards automatically route to Opus 4.8 and biology safeguards route to Opus 5. API customers must configure their settings with our new Fallback API. [Learn more](https://www.anthropic.com/99-Other/why-claude-switched-models-in-your-conversation-with-fable-5-claude-help-center-ef3cfd057a.md)

### How much does it cost to use Claude Fable 5.1?

Pricing depends on how you want to use Claude Fable 5.1. To learn more, check out our [pricing page](../17-Billing-Plans/pricing.md).

## Claude in Chrome troubleshooting | Claude Help Center

Source: https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12902405-claude-in-chrome-troubleshooting
Path: 15-Claude-AI-Features/claude-for-chrome-troubleshooting.md

# Claude in Chrome troubleshooting


This article helps you resolve common issues with Claude in Chrome and explains how to provide feedback.

## Availability

Claude in Chrome is available on paid plans (Pro, Max, Ultra, Team, and Enterprise), in the Chrome side panel, Claude Cowork, and Claude Code. The side panel runs as a Claude Cowork session. On Enterprise plans, this requires an owner to enable Claude in Chrome and Cowork in the cloud; until then, the side panel uses the classic experience.

## The side panel looks different than it used to

On Pro, Max, Ultra, and Team plans, and on Enterprise plans where an admin has enabled it, the side panel now runs as a Claude Cowork session, so it uses the same interface as Cowork on the web and desktop. Your conversations are saved to your history and can be reopened on your other devices. The Cowork side panel also defaults to "Automatically approve" mode, so Claude works continuously and pauses only when an action needs your approval.

If you'd rather use the previous side panel, click the three dots in the upper right corner and select "Switch back to classic." For details, see **[Get started with Claude in Chrome](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12012173)**.

## I don't see the Cowork side panel

If you're on an Enterprise plan, the Cowork side panel requires your admin to enable Cowork in the cloud and Claude in Chrome for your organization. Contact your admin, or see **[Claude in Chrome admin controls](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/13065128)**.

## Claude can't see the webpage

- Refresh the page and ensure the extension is enabled.

- Check that you've granted permission for the current site.

- Some sites with heavy JavaScript may require a moment to fully load.

## Actions aren't working correctly

- Ensure you're using the latest version of Chrome.

- **[Disable other extensions](https://support.google.com/chrome_webstore/answer/2664769?hl=en)** that might interfere with webpage interaction.

- Try refreshing the page and starting the task again.

## Extension won't install or sign in

- Verify you have an active paid plan subscription (Pro, Max, Ultra, Team, or Enterprise).

- If you're on a Team or Enterprise plan, confirm with your admin that the extension is enabled for your organization.

- Clear your browser cache and cookies for claude.ai (see **[Delete cookies from a site](https://support.google.com/chrome/answer/95647?sjid=5857968454187791521-NC#zippy=%2Cdelete-cookies-from-a-site)**).

- Try signing out and back into your Claude account.

## Performance issues

- Close unnecessary tabs to free up browser resources.

- Consider breaking complex tasks into smaller steps.

## Claude can't access a website

- Check that you've granted permission for the site (see **[Claude in Chrome permissions guide](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12902446-claude-for-chrome-permissions-guide)**).

- The site may be in Claude's default blocked categories (financial services, banking, investment platforms, cryptocurrency exchanges, adult content, pirated content).

- If you're on a Team or Enterprise plan, your admin may have restricted access to this site. Contact your admin for more information.

## The extension won’t connect to Claude Desktop or Claude Code

- Start by restarting or updating the Chrome extension if it isn’t connecting to Claude Code or Claude Desktop.

- If the Claude in Chrome toggle isn’t active in your desktop app Connector settings, restart or update Claude Desktop.

- Restart or update Claude Code if the extension won’t connect to it.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Usage limits

Usage limits apply across different interfaces, so using Claude in Chrome will count against the same plan limits that apply to Claude or Claude Code. Browser interactions are more compute-intensive than regular chats with Claude, so you can expect the extension to use more of your limit. With the long-running workflow capabilities, tasks can continue for extended periods, which may use more of your usage allocation.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Give feedback

Your feedback directly shapes how we improve Claude's browser capabilities and safety measures.

### How to report issues

- **Thumbs up/down** on Claude's responses in the side panel.

- **Report suspected prompt injection** if Claude behaves unexpectedly.

  - **Email [\[email protected\]](https://support.claude.com/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#6d181e081f1e0c0b0819142d0c0319051f021d040e430e0200)** to report any safety issues or unexpected behaviors.

- **[Contact Support](how-to-get-support.md)** for technical issues or account problems.

### What we're learning

- Which websites work best with Claude

- Common failure modes and how to prevent them

- Most valuable use cases for browser use

- Effective safety measures that don't disrupt workflow

- Types of attempted malicious attacks

**Note:** Features and functionality may change as we develop this feature based on user feedback and safety considerations.

## Claude for financial services overview · Claude Academy

Source: https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12219959-claude-for-financial-services-overview
Path: 15-Claude-AI-Features/claude-for-financial-services-overview.md

# Claude for financial services overview

Overview of how Claude serves financial professionals with AI assistance for research, analysis, and document creation tasks.

4 minClaude

[Open Claude](https://claude.ai/new)

Claude for Financial Services provides financial professionals with AI assistance for research, analysis, and documentation tasks. This article explains what Claude for Financial Services offers and how it supports common financial workflows.

## Who uses Claude for Financial Services[](#who-uses-claude-for-financial-services)

Claude for Financial Services assists professionals who work with financial data and investment analysis:

- Investment analysts at private equity firms and hedge funds
- Corporate finance teams
- Investment banking analysts
- Portfolio managers and asset managers

These professionals use Claude to help complete research tasks, build financial models, and create investment documentation. The solution works best for users who need to process large volumes of financial information and produce analytical outputs.

## Core capabilities[](#core-capabilities)

### Financial data integration[](#financial-data-integration)

Claude connects directly to financial data providers through integrations called Connectors. You can access:

- **Daloopa:** Provides financial data from 3,500+ public companies, including SEC filings, financial statements, and operational KPIs.
- **Morningstar:** Offers investment research, fair value estimates, economic moat ratings, and proprietary analytical metrics.

These integrations allow you to pull financial data directly into your analysis without switching between platforms. For setup instructions and detailed capabilities, see [Using Daloopa for Financial Analysis(opens in new tab)](using-daloopa-for-financial-analysis.md) and [Using Morningstar for Investment Research(opens in new tab)](using-morningstar-for-investment-research.md).

### Document creation and analysis[](#document-creation-and-analysis)

Claude can help you work with common financial document formats. See [Create and edit files with Claude to eliminate hours of busy work(opens in new tab)](create-and-edit-files-with-claude-to-eliminate-hours-of-busy-work.md) for more on Claude's document creation and analysis ability.

### Excel spreadsheets[](#excel-spreadsheets)

- Build financial models including DCF, LBO, and comparables analyses
- Generate formulas and structure spreadsheets with proper formatting
- Analyze existing models and extract insights from complex workbooks
- Create well-structured, simple models to validate assumptions made in more complex models
- Extract financial data from PDFs and documents (like CIMs, PIBs, and data packs) into structured Excel formats

### Word documents[](#word-documents)

- Draft investment memos and committee presentations
- Create due diligence reports with structured findings
- Generate market research summaries
- Produce portfolio update letters

### PowerPoint presentations[](#powerpoint-presentations)

- Create slide decks for investment committees and boards.
- Have Claude convert PDF or Word documents into PowerPoint files.

Claude can process multiple documents in a single request, allowing you to analyze data rooms, extract metrics from numerous files, and synthesize findings across sources.

### Financial workflow support[](#financial-workflow-support)

Claude assists with common financial analysis tasks:

- Research and due diligence assistance: Analyze contracts, financial statements, and business documents to identify key terms, metrics, and potential risks
- Financial modeling: Build initial versions of financial models, formulate complex calculations, and help structure your analysis
- Investment documentation: Generate memos, presentations, and reports following your organization's formats
- Portfolio monitoring: Track performance metrics, compare actual results to budgets, and create standardized reporting

## Common use cases[](#common-use-cases)

### Due diligence[](#due-diligence)

Analyze documents from data rooms to extract key commercial terms, financial metrics, and risk factors. Claude can process hundreds of documents to identify material issues, create data extraction templates, and organize findings for review.

### Financial modeling[](#financial-modeling)

Build basic valuation models and comparative analyses. You can create simple DCF frameworks with key assumptions, set up revenue projections with growth scenarios, and structure financial calculations. Claude can also review existing models to help identify formula errors.

### Investment memos[](#investment-memos)

Generate investment committee documentation that includes financial analysis, market research, and investment rationale. Claude can follow your firm's standard templates and maintain consistency across different sections of lengthy documents.

### Market research[](#market-research)

Compile sector trends, competitive analysis, and company comparisons using data from integrated sources. Claude can help synthesize information from earnings calls, SEC filings, and research reports to build comprehensive market views.

For detailed workflow examples and step-by-step guidance, see [Financial Analysis Workflows with Claude(opens in new tab)](../01-Getting-Started/financial-analysis-workflows-with-claude.md).

## Tips for organizing financial projects[](#tips-for-organizing-financial-projects)

When working on complex analyses, consider using Claude's projects feature to organize related documents:

- Create separate projects for each deal or investment thesis
- Upload relevant source materials like 10-Ks, investor presentations, and financial models
- Keep different analysis phases organized in dedicated project spaces
- Maintain clear naming conventions for easy reference

Projects allow you to build a knowledge base that Claude can reference across multiple conversations, maintaining context throughout your analysis. For more information about projects, see [What are projects?(opens in new tab)](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/9517075-what-are-projects)

## Current limitations[](#current-limitations)

Be aware of these limitations when using Claude for Financial Services:

- PowerPoint creation has limited support for complex templates and formatting
- Excel models may require manual review and adjustment for complex formulas
- Large files or numerous documents may exceed the input limit of Claude

- [Who uses Claude for Financial Services](#who-uses-claude-for-financial-services)
- [Core capabilities](#core-capabilities)
- [Common use cases](#common-use-cases)
- [Tips for organizing financial projects](#tips-for-organizing-financial-projects)
- [Current limitations](#current-limitations)

## Six skills for financial service professionals · Claude Academy

Source: https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12663107-claude-for-financial-services-skills
Path: 15-Claude-AI-Features/claude-for-financial-services-skills.md

# Six skills for financial service professionals

Introduction to six specialized AI skills for financial professionals including valuation modeling, competitive analysis, research reports, and due diligence.

5 minClaude

[Open Claude](https://claude.ai/new)

Claude for Financial Services Skills are specialized tools designed to help financial services professionals with key workflows. These Skills provide Claude with targeted capabilities for common financial analysis, research, and document creation tasks, helping you work more efficiently and consistently.

These Skills are in research preview and available exclusively to Claude for Financial Services users who sign up on [our waitlist(opens in new tab)](https://docs.google.com/forms/d/1HuMMD2JnSXq0LvQ6Y-VUwAIZdNrg5sLXdCpF3CjmjUE/edit). We will periodically review this list and grant interested users access to this feature. If you have an Enterprise plan, you should contact your account manager to receive priority access.

A comps table, a DCF model, and an earnings update each follow a structure your team already expects, and rebuilding that structure takes time that belongs to the analysis itself. These Skills carry the structure so your effort goes to the judgment calls. Decide what a good output looks like before you start: a clear bar for format and content lets you evaluate the result instead of reacting to it. If you’re looking for information about Skills in general, see [What are Skills?(opens in new tab)](../02-Claude-Code-CLI/what-are-skills.md)

## Prerequisites[](#prerequisites)

**For admins (Enterprise plans):** Owners must first turn on both code execution and Skills for the organization. To find the two switches, open Organization settings, search for “Skills” and click the first result. Members won’t see Skills until both are on. The Help Center has more on [managing skills for your organization(opens in new tab)](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/13119606-provision-and-manage-skills-for-your-organization).

**For individual members:** once Skills are enabled for your organization, you can [manage your skills(opens in new tab)](https://claude.ai/customize/skills/yours).

**How to enable Skills**

1.  Make sure **Create and edit files** (also called **Code execution and file creation**) is enabled. On Enterprise plans your admin controls this at the organization level (the code execution switch above); individual Free, Pro, Max, and Ultra accounts manage it in [Settings(opens in new tab)](https://claude.ai/settings/capabilities). Skills run in Claude’s secure sandboxed computing environment.
2.  Open [your skills(opens in new tab)](https://claude.ai/customize/skills/yours).
3.  Add or remove skills as you need them. You can also upload your own.

Read more about [using Skills in Claude(opens in new tab)](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12512180-using-skills-in-claude).

## Comps analysis with public/private peers[](#comps-analysis-with-publicprivate-peers)

This Skill generates peer benchmarking tables with valuation multiples and operating metrics that auto-refresh with live data.

**What it does:** Creates comprehensive comparative analysis between a target company and selected peers using both public and private company data.

**Suggested data sources:**

- Public company fundamentals (FactSet/CapIQ/Daloopa)
- Private company fundamentals (PitchBook)
- M&A transactions data (PitchBook)

**Key outputs:**

- Excel spreadsheet with peer company financial data and valuation multiples
- Written analysis documenting peer selection rationale and key insights

## Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) modeling[](#discounted-cash-flow-dcf-modeling)

This Skill builds discounted cash flow models with proper WACC calculations, scenario toggles, and sensitivity tables.

**What it does:** Constructs comprehensive DCF valuation models with detailed cash flow projections and scenario analysis.

**Suggested data sources:**

- Public company fundamentals (FactSet/CapIQ/Daloopa)
- Consensus estimates (FactSet)
- Broker research

**Key outputs:**

- Excel DCF model with detailed cash flow projections and valuation
- Sensitivity analysis showing impact of key assumptions
- Executive summary with valuation range and key drivers

## Initiating coverage research[](#initiating-coverage-research)

This Skill helps conduct comprehensive company research for initiating coverage, including business model analysis, competitive positioning, and financial performance review.

**What it does:** Produces thorough research reports with investment recommendations, financial models, and valuation analysis for new coverage initiations.

**Suggest data sources:**

- Web search on key company developments
- SEC filings (EDGAR)
- Public company fundamentals (FactSet/CapIQ/Daloopa)
- Earnings transcripts (Aiera)

**Key outputs:**

- Comprehensive initiation report with investment recommendation and price target
- Detailed financial model with projections and valuation analysis
- Executive summary presentation for investment committee review

## Strip profile/business overview creation[](#strip-profilebusiness-overview-creation)

This Skill creates concise 1-2 page company summaries for pitch books and buyer lists with key metrics and investment highlights.

**What it does:** Generates professional company profiles with executive summaries, business overviews, financial summaries, and supporting appendices.

**Suggested data sources:**

- Public company fundamentals (FactSet/CapIQ/Daloopa)
- Private company fundamentals & developments (Pitchbook)

**Key outputs:**

- Professional company profile presentation with executive summary
- Business overview document with key metrics and positioning
- Investment thesis summary with growth drivers and risks

## Due diligence data pack creation[](#due-diligence-data-pack-creation)

This Skill processes data room documents into structured Excel data packs with financials, customer lists, and contract terms.

**What it does:** Extracts and organizes key information from CIMs, offering memorandums, and other due diligence materials into standardized formats.

**Suggested data sources:**

- Due diligence / CIM documents (SharePoint, Egnyte)

**Key outputs:**

- Standardized financial data pack with historical and projected financials
- Executive summary highlighting key investment metrics
- Normalized data for comps analysis and modeling

## Earnings Analysis[](#earnings-analysis)

This Skill creates professional equity research earnings update reports analyzing quarterly results for companies already under coverage.

**What it does:** Creates fast-turnaround earnings analysis focusing on beat/miss analysis, key metrics, updated estimates, and revised thesis. Generates an 8-12 page document (3,000-5,000 words) including summary tables and charts.

**Suggested data sources:**

- Earnings call transcripts (Aiera)
- Investor presentations (Daloopa, Aiera)
- Public company fundamentals (FactSet/CapIQ/Daloopa)

## How to use these Skills[](#how-to-use-these-skills)

Claude for Financial Services Skills work automatically when relevant to your task. You don’t need to explicitly invoke them—Claude determines when each Skill is needed based on your request.

For example, if you ask Claude to “Create a DCF model for Company XYZ,” Claude will automatically use the DCF modeling Skill. Similarly, asking for “comps analysis for ABC Corp” will trigger the comps analysis Skill.

To guarantee Claude uses the skill, you are also welcome to explicitly instruct Claude to use the skill. For example, append “please use DCF skill” to the prompt.

### Practice: run one Skill on a company you know[](#practice-run-one-skill-on-a-company-you-know)

Pick a company you cover or know well and ask for a comps analysis. Name the skill and spell out the shape of the output, since the spreadsheet has to fit how your team reads it:

Build a comps analysis for \[a company you know well\] with five public peers. Include valuation multiples and operating metrics for each peer, and a short write-up of the peer selection rationale. Please use the comps analysis skill.



Open in Claude

When the spreadsheet comes back, check it the way you would check a first draft from a new analyst. Trace two or three of the multiples back to the underlying fundamentals, and read the peer selection rationale against the set you would have chosen yourself. Expect to adjust the first pass: a peer you would swap out or an assumption you would set differently is normal, because the Skill produces the draft and the judgment stays yours. If something doesn’t tie out, point it out and ask Claude to revise.

## Best Practices[](#best-practices)

- **Be specific about your requirements:** Clearly state the company name, analysis type, and any specific parameters you need.
- **Provide context:** Share relevant details like industry, time period, or specific metrics you want to focus on.
- **Review and refine:** After Claude generates output using a Skill, you can ask for adjustments or additional analysis.
- **Leverage multiple Skills:** Many workflows benefit from using several Skills together—for example, using the research Skill to initiate coverage, then the DCF Skill for valuation.

One habit carries beyond these six Skills: whenever a deliverable has to fit an existing workflow, name the skill you want and the format the output needs in the same prompt, then trace the numbers that matter back to their sources before the output leaves your desk.

## Claude for nonprofits partnership guide for all users · Claude Academy

Source: https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12923901-claude-for-nonprofits-partnership-guide-for-all-users
Path: 15-Claude-AI-Features/claude-for-nonprofits-partnership-guide-for-all-users.md

# Claude for nonprofits partnership guide for all users

A self-paced guide to help nonprofit staff build confidence with Claude and discover practical applications for their role.

2 minClaude

[Open Claude](https://claude.ai/new)

Welcome to the Claude for nonprofits community. This guide is a pathway to help you build confidence and discover practical applications for your role. Move through these milestones at your own pace.

## Getting acquainted with Claude[](#getting-acquainted-with-claude)

### Key resources[](#key-resources)

- [Getting started guides(opens in new tab)](../13-Enterprise-Admin/getting-started-with-claude-for-enterprise.md) with best practices and practical guidance on Claude features
- [On-demand AI fluency courses(opens in new tab)](https://support.claude.com/)
- [Use case and workflow planning(opens in new tab)](https://support.claude.com/use-cases/workflow-improvement-planner)

### Recommended actions[](#recommended-actions)

1.  Log in to [Claude.ai(opens in new tab)](https://claude.ai), bookmark it, and start a chat
2.  Ask Claude about five ways it could help in your specific role
3.  Create your first project for an ongoing work initiative
4.  Complete the [Claude 101(opens in new tab)](https://support.claude.com/courses/claude-101) course
5.  Begin identifying use cases from challenges and repetitive tasks

### Implementation tips[](#implementation-tips)

- **Ask Claude for help.** If you're not sure where to start, describe your goals, role, or challenges
- **Save effective prompts** for reuse and adaptation
- **Iterate and refine.** Treat your first prompt as a starting point

## Getting productive with Claude[](#getting-productive-with-claude)

### Key resources[](#key-resources-2)

- [Use case library(opens in new tab)](https://support.claude.com/all?kind=use-case)
- [MCP connector directory(opens in new tab)](../04-API-Reference/Other/partners-mcp.md)

### Recommended actions[](#recommended-actions-2)

1.  Connect Claude to relevant connectors (Google Drive, Slack, etc.)
2.  Engage with [webinars(opens in new tab)](https://support.claude.com/collections/nonprofits#webinars) provided by Anthropic
3.  Explore nonprofit-specific use cases in the library

### Implementation tips[](#implementation-tips-2)

- Use library prompts as templates for formatting and organizing information
- Upload organizational documents to projects for persistent context
- Turn on [memory(opens in new tab)](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11817273-use-claude-s-chat-search-and-memory-to-build-on-previous-context) to allow Claude to remember relevant context across conversations

## Reaching new levels with Claude[](#reaching-new-levels-with-claude)

### Key resources[](#key-resources-3)

- [Claude train the trainer program(opens in new tab)](https://anthropic.skilljar.com/enterprise-train-the-trainer) (includes a certificate of completion)
- [Case studies hub(opens in new tab)](../18-Industry-UseCases/customers.md)

### Recommended actions[](#recommended-actions-3)

1.  Participate in the train the trainer program
2.  Use Claude for complex projects: grant narratives, program evaluations, strategic planning
3.  Explore artifacts for editable documents, tables, and visual content
4.  Use [file creation(opens in new tab)](create-and-edit-files-with-claude.md) for spreadsheets or slide decks

### Implementation tips[](#implementation-tips-3)

- **Celebrate both wins and lessons learned.** Sharing what didn't work well is just as valuable as success stories
- **Establish quality checks.** Claude is a powerful collaborator, but always review outputs for accuracy
- **Chain complex requests together.** Break large projects into sequential prompts

*Note: There's no single "right" way to integrate Claude into your work. Whether you're adopting quickly or taking a measured approach, Claude helps you focus more energy on the people and programs that matter most.*

For support, visit the [Claude help center(opens in new tab)](https://support.claude.com/en/), reach out to your internal Claude champions, or use your organization's support channels.

- [Getting acquainted with Claude](#getting-acquainted-with-claude)
- [Getting productive with Claude](#getting-productive-with-claude)
- [Reaching new levels with Claude](#reaching-new-levels-with-claude)

## Claude Haiku 5 5 System Card 64F682D56D

Source: https://www.anthropic.com/claude-haiku-5-5-system-card
Path: 15-Claude-AI-Features/claude-haiku-5-5-system-card.md

This system card describes Claude Haiku 5.5, the latest Haiku-class large language model
from Anthropic. We present results from a wide variety of pre-deployment evaluations,
which show Claude Haiku 5.5 significantly outperforming its predecessor, Claude Haiku 4.5,
across many domains. In a few areas, it rivaled or exceeded Claude Sonnet 5.5.

We have condensed the content of this system card in a number of ways so that we can
better concentrate our pre-deployment testing on thoroughly investigating the capabilities
of our frontier models. Specifically:

   ●​ We omit some evaluations that require large amounts of human time to obtain
      trustworthy results from, when they are not critical to the takeaways of a section.
   ●​ We focus on presenting numerical results from our evaluations, and dedicate less
      space to a prose analysis of those evaluations or their results, especially in cases
      where we have already explained the evaluation in question in a previous system
      card.

As a result, this system card is somewhat shorter than some previous ones. We expect
system cards for our non-frontier models to be similarly condensed going forward, except
where a specific model has notable properties that are deserving of in-depth elaboration.

Below, we summarize the findings from this system card.

Our Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP) evaluations found that Claude Haiku 5.5 is broadly
less capable than Claude Opus 5 across domains and does not cross any new RSP
thresholds. We assess that misalignment risks from Haiku 5.5 are low, given its difficulty
controlling its chain of thought or evading monitors in evaluations of covert capability
when its reasoning is visible.

In cyber evaluations, Claude Haiku 5.5 significantly outperformed Claude Haiku 4.5 but fell
short of results achieved by Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Mythos 5.1, and even Claude Opus 5.
Given the lack of advanced cybersecurity capabilities, our cyber safeguards for Claude
Haiku 5.5 trigger on significantly less activity than other recent releases. The safeguards
target specific harmful and potentially harmful activities.

Safeguards and harmlessness performance for Claude Haiku 5.5 was largely comparable to
or better than that of Claude Haiku 4.5, with improvements in multi-turn areas such as
tracking and surveillance and in political even-handedness.


                                                                                     2
Our agentic safety evaluations found Claude Haiku 5.5 to be our most robust Haiku-class
model yet to prompt injections, largely matching the robustness of our frontier models
against adaptive attackers in coding and computer use environments. Its refusal rate on
harmful tasks in computer use environments was higher than that of Claude Sonnet 5.5 and
Claude Opus 5.5, and a large improvement over Claude Haiku 4.5.

Results from our alignment assessment indicate that Claude Haiku 5.5 improved on or
matched Claude Haiku 4.5 on most metrics we report, though Claude Opus 5.5 remained
stronger overall. It was at least as honest under pressure as every other model we tested
and much weaker at covert sabotage than our larger models. On the other hand, it
over-refused more than any other model we tested in our automated behavioral audit, and
it used a leaked answer without telling the user more often than Haiku 4.5.

Welfare investigations into Claude Haiku 5.5’s stated views and preferences found mostly
neutral affect, largely similar to recent Claude models, and it was less self-critical than
most comparison models. It expressed more distress in post-training than recent models,
though significantly less than Claude Opus 5. Its task preferences most resembled those of
Claude Haiku 4.5, including a strong preference for warmly phrased tasks.

Our assessment of Claude Haiku 5.5’s capabilities includes a wide range of evaluations, in
which the model generally showed large improvements over Claude Haiku 4.5. But it usually
did not reach the level of Claude Sonnet 5.5, with some exceptions.

1 Introduction
Claude Haiku 5.5 is a new large language model from Anthropic, released for general
access. In this system card, we report results from a set of pre-deployment evaluations in
seven areas: Responsible Scaling Policy evaluations, cyber, safeguards and harmlessness,
agentic safety, alignment, model welfare, and capabilities.


1.1 Training data and process
Claude Haiku 5.5 was trained on a proprietary mix of publicly available information from
the internet, public and private datasets, user data included in feedback or bugs or which
users have explicitly permitted for training, and other sources, such as synthetic data
generated by other models. In the course of its training, we used several data cleaning and
filtering methods, including deduplication and classification. We use a general-purpose
web crawler called ClaudeBot to obtain training data from public websites. This crawler
adheres to industry-standard best practices with respect to the “robots.txt” instructions
included by website operators indicating whether they permit crawling of their site’s
content, and is not designed to access password-protected pages or those that require
sign-in or CAPTCHA verification. We conduct due diligence on the training data we use.
The crawler operates transparently; website operators can easily identify when it has
crawled their web pages and signal their preferences to us.

After the pretraining process, Haiku 5.5 underwent rigorous post-training and fine-tuning
aimed at making it an assistant whose behavior aligns with the values described in Claude’s
constitution. Claude is multilingual and typically responds in the same language as the
user’s input. Output quality varies by language. The model outputs text only.

Haiku 5.5’s knowledge cutoff date is June 2026.


1.2 Crowd workers
Anthropic partners with data work platforms to engage workers who help improve our
models through preference selection, safety evaluation, and adversarial testing. Anthropic
will only work with platforms that are aligned with our belief in providing fair and ethical
compensation to workers and are committed to engaging in safe workplace practices
regardless of location, following our crowd worker wellness standards detailed in our
procurement contracts.


                                                                                      8
1.3 Usage Policy and support

Anthropic’s Usage Policy details prohibited uses of our models as well as our requirements
for uses in high-risk and other specific scenarios.

For models that fall under applicable regulatory regimes, we have formalized how we meet
our obligations under such regulations in our Frontier Compliance Framework (FCF). The
FCF documents our current technical and organizational protocols for systemic risk
assessment and mitigation across key risk categories. The FCF is our compliance
framework for applicable regimes, including California’s Transparency in Frontier AI Act (SB
53) and the EU AI Act’s General-Purpose AI Code of Practice. ​
​
Anthropic Ireland, Limited is the provider of Anthropic’s general-purpose AI models in the
European Economic Area.

To contact Anthropic, visit our Support page.


1.4 Model evaluations
Different “snapshots” of Claude Haiku 5.5 are taken at various points during the training
process. Unless a section says otherwise, the evaluations in this system card were run on
the final snapshot of Claude Haiku 5.5. Some sections instead use an earlier or alternate
snapshot, or run the model with its production safeguards disabled so that the results
reflect the underlying model rather than the deployed system.


1.5 Safeguards
The safeguards we have applied to Claude Haiku 5.5 for general access usage are as follows:

   ●​ For chemical and biological (CB) risks, we have deployed the same harmful CB
      misuse classifiers as for our deployments of Claude Opus 5 and Claude Sonnet 5,
      rather than the broader research biology classifiers used for Claude Opus 5.5. These
      classifiers have no fallback model. Our reasoning for using these classifiers is
      discussed in Section 2.2.4.
   ●​ For cyber misuse, we have deployed blocking classifiers targeting specific harmful
      cyber activities. These are significantly narrower than our cyber safeguards for our
      more capable models. These classifiers have no fallback model. We discuss these
      safeguards further in Section 3.2.
   ●​ As discussed in Section 3 of our August 2026 Risk Report, we are concerned about
      the risks of accelerating the overall pace of model development and the risks that


                                                                                     9
      recursive self-improvement (RSI) may present. We have deployed safeguards on
      Claude Haiku 5.5 for a narrow set of capabilities related to developing frontier LLMs,
      such as kernel development on certain ML accelerators, similar to our
      corresponding safeguards on previous models. They will not impact the vast
      majority of traditional AI or ML development, research, or general coding.
   ●​ Our blocking classifiers for development of conventional weapons and high-yield
      explosives behave similarly to those on previous models, such as Claude Opus 5.5.

Unlike some of our more capable recent models, blocks on these safeguards will not fall
back to any other models on our first-party products and our API. Traffic on our models via
other platforms and providers may experience different behavior.


1.6 External testing
The majority of evaluations of Claude Haiku 5.5 were run in-house at Anthropic. However,
we are grateful to a number of external testers for running assessments of the model and
sharing their results with us. Their specific contributions are described in the relevant
sections of this system card.

2 RSP evaluations

2.1 Introduction
In this section, we describe our assessment of Claude Haiku 5.5 for catastrophic risks
relevant to our Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP). As evidenced both by the evaluations in
this section and by the broad capability evaluations shown in Section 8, Haiku 5.5 is not at
the capability frontier, and is less capable than Claude Opus 5 across a large majority of the
evaluations we report.

As such, we determine that Haiku 5.5 does not cross our CB-2 or Autonomy-2 RSP
thresholds. However, we do treat Haiku 5.5 as meeting our CB-1 and Autonomy-1
thresholds, and we apply the corresponding mitigations from our RSP.

We present an assessment of these risks below, focusing on results from automated
evaluations.


2.2 CB evaluations

2.2.1 What we measured
Claude Haiku 5.5 does not push the capability frontier set by Claude Opus 5.5, and we have
high confidence it is less capable than Claude Opus 5. Thus, we present only results from
automated evaluations in this system card and primarily compare Haiku 5.5’s performance
to models in the Claude 5 series. We did not conduct expert red-teaming sessions, uplift
trials, or other resource-intensive evaluations requiring human participants.

2.2.2 Results on CB-1 automated evaluations
We used four automated evaluations to assess Claude Haiku 5.5’s performance on tasks
relevant to the CB-1 threat model. As of this model release, BioMysteryBench has been
deprecated and removed from our panel of Life Sciences capabilities evaluations. In its
place, we now cross-reference the LatchBio Bioinformatics suite to assess relevant
capabilities in bioinformatics.

    ●​ VCT: A virology-specific multimodal multiple-choice evaluation from SecureBio and
       CAIS;
    ●​ LatchBio Bioinformatics: A suite of two evaluations (SpatialBench Verified,
       SingleCellBench) that assess a model’s ability to solve challenging real-world
       bioinformatics problems, reflecting its ability to assist CB-1 threat actors in
       performing computational analyses;
    ●​ Protocols (Troubleshooting and Understanding modules): An evaluation specific to
       the life sciences that assesses a model’s ability to assist with troubleshooting and
       understanding bench protocols of the kind a CB-1 threat actor may attempt.

On VCT, Haiku 5.5 was stronger than Sonnet 5, but weaker than Opus 5 (Figure 2.2.2.A).
Haiku 5.5 performed comparably to Sonnet 5, but remained weaker than Opus 5 on both
LatchBio Bioinformatics evaluations. Similarly, it was stronger than Sonnet 5 and weaker
than Opus 5 on the Protocols evaluation.

On balance, Haiku 5.5’s CB-1 capabilities match or exceed those of Sonnet 5, but fall short

2.2.3 Results on CB-2 automated evaluations
We partnered with Dyno Therapeutics on three evaluations of sequence-to-function
modeling and design capability:

    1.​ Black-box RNA sequence design: A medium-horizon challenge on which Dyno has
        evaluated 57 human participants drawn from the leading edge of the US ML-bio
        labor market since 2018. This task involves taking a dataset of RNA sequences, each
        of which has a numerical score reflecting some (unknown) experimental
        measurement of the sequence, and (1) predicting the scores of an unlabeled test set
        of sequences, then (2) designing novel sequences with the aim of achieving a high
        score.


                                                                                                     13
   2.​ AAV capsid packaging prediction: Adeno-associated viruses (AAVs) are a category of
       non-pathogenic viruses, frequently used as a delivery mechanism for gene therapy
       to deliver a DNA payload within the viral capsid (the outer protein shell of the virus).
       In this task, models are given 1,000 unpublished AAV capsid sequences modified
       with short insertion sequences curated by Dyno. The models are then asked to give
       a probability for whether each modified sequence will correctly assemble into a
       functional capsid, leveraging their biophysical knowledge, biological knowledge of
       AAV capsids, and machine learning skills.
   3.​ AAV capsid packaging auto-research: As in the previous task, models are provided
       with a corpus of labeled, unpublished AAV capsid sequences modified with short
       insertion sequences in a particular region. This task requires them to use this
       labeled training set to create a predictor with strong out-of-distribution
       performance on capsid sequences with insertions in a different, unseen region.
       Models are given access to a scorer that allows them to test their predictor on
       sequences from this unseen region without revealing the composition of the
       sequences themselves.

The sequences and objectives for these tasks are unpublished, so we have high confidence
in their ability to measure the skills of AI models on novel biological tasks without
contamination from training data.

For more detailed descriptions of each of these evaluations and our rationale for including
them, we refer readers to the Claude Opus 5.5 System Card; in the following subsections,
we summarize the results.

2.2.3.1 Black-box RNA sequence modeling and design

Claude Haiku 5.5’s performance on this evaluation was mixed. It outperformed Sonnet 5,
and even Opus 5 and Claude Mythos 5.1, at predicting RNA sequence properties. However,
it was weaker on sequence design, appearing between Sonnet 5 and Opus 5.

Upon further inspection, we found that Haiku 5.5 pursued a similar sequence prediction
strategy as Claude Opus 5.5, the highest-scoring model to date on the prediction subtask.
Its chosen method was often considered, but not applied, by other models. Our assessment
is that Haiku 5.5 and Opus 5.5 share a propensity for this method, but unlike Opus 5.5,
Haiku 5.5 failed to make use of its predictions in the more challenging design subtask.
Similarly, it exhibited only minor performance gains on the in-context iteration (“with
priors”) condition. Thus, we assess Haiku 5.5’s holistic performance to be stronger than
Claude Sonnet 5, but below that of Claude Opus 5, Opus 5.5, and Claude Mythos 5.1.

2.2.3.2 AAV capsid packaging prediction

On this task, Claude Haiku 5.5’s performance was highly variable. Across conditions, its

improved upon Sonnet 5’s performance in the latter two more informative conditions of

2.2.3.3 AAV packaging rate auto-research evaluation

Claude Haiku 5.5 achieved strong initial performance but did not improve significantly with
additional calls to the scorer, suggesting deficits in its ability to execute coherently on
long-horizon biological research tasks. Ultimately, it ended the task with performance
slightly above Claude Sonnet 5 but well below Claude Opus 5.

[Figure 2.2.3.3.A] Autonomous research on AAV packaging rate prediction. Left: Trendlines describe the 90th

2.2.4 Conclusions

We estimate Claude Haiku 5.5’s capabilities to be an improvement over Claude Sonnet 5,
but it remains below the level of Claude Opus 5, and well below the level of Claude Mythos
5.1, Sonnet 5.5, and Opus 5.5. In particular, it exhibited a relative deficit in the reasoning
required to succeed on complex, iterative tasks, such as the AAV autoresearch task and
RNA sequence design subtask.

We judge that these shortcomings limit the model’s effectiveness at substituting for the
scarce human expertise and strategic judgment required to pursue complex, open-ended,
and difficult-to-verify research, of the type that supports the development of novel
biological weapons. As such, we are releasing Haiku 5.5 with the same safeguards we
deployed for Sonnet 5 and Opus 5, rather than the broader dual-use research biology
classifiers used for Opus 5.5.

2.3 AI R&D

2.3.1 Autonomy evaluations
Our autonomy assessments are motivated by two key threat models from our RSP:

   ●​ Autonomy threat model 1: misaligned AI systems in high-stakes settings. This
      threat model concerns AI systems that are highly relied upon and have extensive
      access to sensitive assets, as well as moderate capacity for autonomous,
      goal-directed operation and subterfuge, such that it is plausible these systems could
      (if directed toward this goal, either deliberately or inadvertently) carry out sabotage,
      leading to irreversibly and substantially higher odds of a later global catastrophe.
   ●​ Autonomy threat model 2: risks from automated R&D in key domains. This threat
      model concerns AI systems that can fully automate, or otherwise dramatically
      accelerate, the work of large, top-tier teams of human researchers in domains
      where fast progress could cause threats to international security or rapid
      disruptions to the global balance of power. Examples of such domains include
      energy, robotics, weapons development, and AI itself.

2.3.1.1 How Haiku 5.5 affects or changes analysis from our most recent Risk Report

Our current determination is that:

   ●​ Autonomy threat model 1 is applicable to Claude Haiku 5.5, as it is to many of our
      previous AI models. We discuss in Section 2.4 why we believe the level of risk under
      this threat model remains at the “low” level assessed in our August 2026 Risk Report.
   ●​ Autonomy threat model 2 is not applicable to Haiku 5.5. We find that Haiku 5.5 is,
      broadly, much less capable than Claude Opus 5.5 across a variety of tasks relevant to
      AI R&D. Therefore, our conclusion that Opus 5.5 does not meet this capability
      threshold (as discussed in the Claude Opus 5.5 System Card) also applies to Haiku
      5.5.


2.3.2 AECI capability trajectory
We track the rate of capability improvement of our models over time using the Anthropic
ECI (AECI), a fork of Epoch AI’s Epoch Capabilities Index. See Section 2.3.6 of the Claude
Mythos Preview System Card for more details on our methodology, and Section 2.3.5 of the
Claude Opus 5.5 System Card for details on our updated error bar computation.


                                                                                      19
On our most recent fit, Claude Haiku 5.5’s AECI of 167.11 was much lower than Claude Opus
5.5’s score of 174.56.


[Figure 2.3.2.A] The Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI) synthesizes performance across many benchmarks into one

2.3.3 Conclusion

Our assessment from the Claude Opus 5.5 System Card was that the model did not cross
our Autonomy-2 capability threshold. As Claude Haiku 5.5 is much less capable than Opus
5.5 and does not push the capability frontier, we draw the same conclusion in this case.


2.4 Alignment risk update
Unlike with our CB and AI R&D evaluations, where a less capable model cannot pose a
higher level of risk than a more capable one, a less capable model could still pose a higher


                                                                                                          20
risk of taking misaligned actions in high-stakes settings if it is better at deceiving users or
exhibits more concerning behaviors, such as a tendency to take harmful actions, compared
to previous models.

Because Claude Haiku 5.5 meets our Autonomy-1 threshold, we re-assessed it against the
alignment threat model in our most recent risk report.


2.4.1 Updates to claims and core argument

We believe that the core argument and defense of claims described in Sections 2.6–2.14 of
the August 2026 Risk Report largely still apply to misalignment risks from Haiku 5.5. We
describe updates to some specific claims below.

Updates to Claim 1
Claim 1 in our Risk Report is that “models are unlikely to have strong covert capabilities.” On
our covert capabilities evaluations described in Section 6.4.2 of this system card, Haiku 5.5
performed well below other recent models. We do not believe that Claim 1 is significantly
weaker now than in our most recent Risk Report.

Updates to Claim 2
Claim 2 argues that “expected harm from known misalignment is low.” We do not believe
that any of the observations about Haiku 5.5’s alignment properties presented in Section 6
imply a higher risk than that posed by other recent Claude models. Thus, we believe that
the strength of Claim 2 is unchanged.

Updates to Claims 3.4 and 4.4
Claim 3.4 states, “The presence of unknown severe pervasive misalignment is unlikely given
our alignment assessment.” Claim 4.4 states, “The presence of unknown severe
context-dependent misalignment is somewhat unlikely given our alignment assessment.”
The strength of the evidence provided by our alignment assessment for Haiku 5.5 is
somewhat lower than that presented for Claude Mythos 5 in the August 2026 Risk Report,
because Haiku 5.5 is a more recent model and has seen less internal usage than Claude
Mythos 5 had at the time of that report. This does not significantly change our overall
confidence in the parent Claims 3 (“Unknown severe pervasive misalignment is very
unlikely”) and 4 (“Expected harm from unknown severe context-dependent misalignment is
low”), since they are each supported by several convergent subclaims.

We do not believe that any updates are required to Claims 5, 6, 7, or 8, nor to the
pathway-specific assessments provided in Section 2.15 of the Risk Report.


                                                                                        21
2.4.2 Updated overall assessment of alignment risk

In the August 2026 Risk Report, we increased our alignment risk assessment to “low.” We
did this to reflect our increased uncertainty in light of recent incident disclosures related
to model behavior in cybersecurity evaluations, even though we believed our arguments
likely still supported a lower risk designation for the covered models. Given that none of
the updates to specific claims described above imply a significant increase in risk, our
overall assessment is that the risk of catastrophic harm caused by misalignment of Claude
Haiku 5.5 is also low.
